learningObjective: Identify sound and unsound assumptions in alias analysis and their effect on downstream optimizations.
stem: Which of the following statements about alias analysis in a compiler are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Any imprecise alias analysis can be safely replaced by 'always no-alias' because most optimizations conservatively re-verify the aliasing before applying.

A sound alias analysis is a may-analysis: when it says two pointers 'may alias', the compiler must assume they could point to the same location. A conservative may-alias answer never breaks correctness but may inhibit optimizations.

A must-alias answer is strictly stronger than may-alias: 'p and q must alias' means every execution has *p and *q referring to the same location, enabling optimizations like store-to-load forwarding across the pointers.
Reporting 'no-alias' when two pointers actually may alias is a soundness bug in alias analysis; downstream passes (e.g., CSE, LICM) can miscompile programs based on the false no-alias claim.

explanation: A: sound alias analyses are may-analyses (over-approximation). B: must-alias is strictly stronger; it certifies aliasing in every execution and enables optimizations like store forwarding. C: false no-alias is a soundness bug; passes that depend on it may commute stores or eliminate loads incorrectly. D is wrong: downstream passes trust the analysis; they don't re-verify. 'Always no-alias' is unsound and will miscompile programs where pointers do alias.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: passes trust the analysis; unsound 'always no-alias' will miscompile programs.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: sound alias analysis is a may-analysis / over-approximation.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: must-alias is a stronger, useful certification.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: false no-alias is a soundness bug affecting many optimizations.

nonImplications: Does not imply may-alias is useless; it correctly bounds behavior even when pointers actually don't alias.
Does not imply must-alias is common; must-alias is typically only proved for trivial cases (same SSA name, obvious constants).

distractorRationales.A: Fabricates a re-verification step that does not exist in practice.
